subtopics.title: Dispute background and positions
subtopics.summary: The Mahanadi dispute concerns how the river's waters are shared between upstream Chhattisgarh and downstream Odisha. Odisha says upstream construction has reduced its downstream flow, while Chhattisgarh cites its larger catchment share and development needs. The conflict is sharpest in the non-monsoon season and is intensified by the absence of a formal sharing agreement.
facts: Dispute escalated around 2016 after increased upstream infrastructure development

Absence of a formal inter-state water-sharing agreement has intensified the conflict

subtopics.title: Tribunal status and deadlock
subtopics.summary: The Mahanadi Water Disputes Tribunal has given both states a final opportunity to agree a water-sharing formula and has issued an ultimatum for a settlement by May 2. If no settlement is reached, the Tribunal will decide on available evidence and legal principles. The Tribunal has voiced dissatisfaction with repeated adjournments, and the deadlock is linked to unreliable data and a trust deficit.

subtopics.title: Legal framework for inter-state waters
subtopics.summary: Article 262 empowers Parliament to adjudicate inter-state river disputes and allows it to exclude courts' jurisdiction in such matters. The Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 was used for the Mahanadi tribunal, and the River Boards Act, 1956 provides for river boards. Entries 17 and 56 divide powers between the States and the Union, and the Supreme Court cannot question a tribunal's award but can question its working.

subtopics.title: River course and Hirakud Dam
subtopics.summary: The Mahanadi originates at Sihawa Hill in Raipur, Chhattisgarh, and flows through Odisha before emptying into the Bay of Bengal. It receives left-bank and right-bank tributaries. Hirakud Dam on the river is described in the booklet as the longest earthen dam in the world.
facts: Mahanadi originates at Sihawa Hill in Raipur, Chhattisgarh
Mahanadi flows through Odisha before emptying into the Bay of Bengal
Left bank tributaries: Shivnath, Hasdeo, Mand and Ib
Right bank tributaries: Jonk, Ong and Tel
Hirakud Dam is the longest earthen dam in the world

subtopics.title: Other inter-state water tribunals
subtopics.summary: India has several inter-state water tribunals, each set up for a particular river dispute. The booklet lists tribunals formed between 1986 and 2018, covering states such as Punjab, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Odisha. The Mahanadi tribunal is one of these five.
facts: Ravi & Beas Water Tribunal, formed 1986: Rajasthan, Haryana and Punjab
Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal II, formed 2004: Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Telangana and Karnataka
Mahadayi Water Disputes Tribunal, formed 2010: Karnataka, Goa and Maharashtra
Vansadhara Water Disputes Tribunal, formed 2010: Odisha and Andhra Pradesh
Mahanadi Water Disputes Tribunal, formed 2018: Chhattisgarh and Odisha

quizzes.passage:
The Mahanadi dispute between Odisha and Chhattisgarh concerns how the river's water is shared, especially in the non-monsoon season, when water flowing downstream becomes critically important. The absence of a formal inter-state water-sharing agreement has added to the conflict, and Odisha has argued that upstream construction in Chhattisgarh has reduced the flow reaching its own territory. Chhattisgarh, for its part, maintains that it has a legitimate right to use river waters and that its projects serve regional development.

Such disputes are handled through a separate arrangement. The Constitution provides for them, and the law built on it allows a tribunal to be set up when a dispute needs adjudication. The tribunal then issues its decision, and the matter is decided on the basis of available evidence and legal principles.

The Mahanadi tribunal has expressed concern about repeated adjournments and the lack of substantive progress in talks. It has observed that no concrete proposals have been placed on record, despite assurances of settlement efforts. The tribunal has therefore given both states a final opportunity to agree on a formula.

Other river disputes in the country have also been handled through tribunals, each set up for a particular river. Read together, these cases show that water sharing between states is governed by a special framework rather than by routine legal channels.

quizzes.passage:
The Mahanadi is at the centre of a long-running dispute because its water supports many activities along its course. Downstream areas rely on the river for irrigation, drinking water, fisheries and the wider ecology of the area. When flow declines, these uses come under strain, and the concern becomes most acute during the non-monsoon season.

The river is fed by a network of tributaries that join it along its length. Its waters therefore reflect conditions across a large catchment, and activities in upstream areas can affect what reaches the lower reaches. Upstream construction is one such activity, and it has been cited as a reason for falling downstream flow. Water reaching any point along the river thus depends on conditions upstream.

Large infrastructure also lies on the river. Among these works is a dam that has been a major point of attention in discussions of the river. The presence of such structures makes it harder to assess the river's flow without reliable information. Such works are discussed in relation to the river's flow and its sharing among states.

The booklet includes a map of the river, which helps readers follow its path through the region. Its course is described in a short section that covers the river's main features. The booklet's summary is brief, so the map and text together give a basic picture of the river.

quizzes.passage:
India has several inter-state water tribunals, and each one has been set up for a particular river dispute. The booklet lists tribunals formed at different points over the years, and each entry links a tribunal to the states involved in that dispute. Several states appear in more than one tribunal, so disputes over different rivers can involve the same state.

The Mahanadi tribunal is one of the bodies in the table. It was set up to resolve the sharing of the Mahanadi's waters between the two states along the river. The tribunal has been dissatisfied with repeated adjournments and a lack of progress, and it has granted both states a final opportunity to reach a formula.

The booklet presents the tribunals in a table with three columns: the name of each tribunal, its year of formation, and the states involved. The table covers five tribunals in total. Each entry records the name, the year and the states, so the table gives a compact summary of the disputes it covers.

Taken together, these entries show that India has used separate tribunals for separate rivers, each tied to its own set of states. The table is part of a wider discussion in the booklet about inter-state river disputes and the legal framework for resolving them.
